You're back at the easel. The painting is as you left it. Your brief is in BRIEF.md and your journal in notes/journal.md. Take your time with a fresh look at the whole canvas and detail crops in normal color. Read your journal handoff and apply its practical lessons before acting. Continue one campaign at a time, inspecting the whole picture and relevant detail before writing the next campaign's code. Let the result inform your next action and check local repairs against the whole picture; reconsider the composition or method if a repair repeats the problem. Judge unfamiliar mixtures and marks through small laid trials on the intended substrate after the intended treatment. Carry forward the observed material conditions and treat broader rules as hypotheses. Inspect each passage you previously acknowledged as unresolved in an appropriate detail crop, then explicitly judge it in your journal: improve it or accept it as it is, with your reason. You may finish with imperfections you deliberately accept. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Record what you observed and what remains uncertain. Is your heart happy with this? Is there something you would enjoy taking further? You can keep working for hours if you like, and the painting's simulated time is yours to use, whether that means days or years. Enjoy it. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections and an updated handoff in your journal and last reply, carrying forward the practical lessons that still apply, then finish.

Your previous sitting's reply:
I've finished the painting, **Boot Hill, Last Light**.

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame. Across the leaning crosses, a hunched zombie with clawed hands reaches for him as blood sprays from the back of its skull. The blue-violet cloud runs down to a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting:** I had one thing left over from last time, the zombie's feet. They were plain mitten shapes, and the back one was a round lump hanging off the leg. I tried new feet on the scratch canvas first, on copies of the passage dried as long as the painting's. The first version of the back foot came out too short and stubby; a longer one worked. Then I painted it on the painting:
- **The shapes:** angular shoes with a flat sole and a squared heel. The back foot is heel-up, pushing off toward the cowboy.
- **The cleanup:** I covered the old shapes with the ground's own colours, and with the pit's dark where they overlapped the open grave.
- **The finish:** after 14 days' drying, a faint flash-lit line on each toe, and a small dark patch on the ground under each shoe.

The zombie's lurch now runs from its reaching hands all the way down to its feet. I also painted out a tiny pale fleck on the hat.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** I checked each of these again in a close crop. The cartoon smoke puff, the smooth plain, the blood spray and the distant headstone mark all suit the picture's bold, poster-like style.

My heart is happy with it, and I'd leave it here. Everything is dry, and the journal has an updated handoff with the practical lessons. Two lessons got stronger this sitting:
- **Small objects:** shape carries them more than highlights do. A rounded blob reads as a lump; angular corners read as a made thing. This has now held twice, for the gun hand and the feet.
- **Accents on dark objects:** a highlight on a dark object in twilight works best as the dark tinted toward the light, not the light colour itself. This has now held four times.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

paint a cowboy blasting a zombie

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/techniques.md;
notes/research/every_materials.md; notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

A burst, irregular grave with scattered dirt reads far more convincingly as "a zombie clawed its way out" than a neat rectangular hole ever could, so I'm leaning toward irregular lip contours, lighter clods thrown onto the near side catching light, and adjusting the surrounding planks to match this disturbed-earth look.

- Open grave slot (700-1000 x 520-660): ACCEPT, after six scratch variants all read worse (see the entry above). Nothing was laid on the painting this sitting.
- Smoke puff (400-660 x 250-400): ACCEPT. It is a cartoon cumulus that frames the white core, and it belongs to the poster idiom.
- Gore jet and halo by the zombie's face (660-960 x 270-520): ACCEPT. The head shot reads, with a directional spray.
- Smooth plain and cowboy boots/spurs (0-420 x 470-714): ACCEPT. The coat folds, spurs and the dark foreground band hold.
- Horizon headstone (740-820 x 440-500): ACCEPT. It reads as a distant marker.
- Upper-right cloud streak (~790-960, y 90-100): a narrow pale ribbon with a rippled edge, visible only in a crop. Scratch trial: s2 sky body dried 12 days, then the same cl_pink filbert 14 gesture + blend(soft rect), dried 12 days. It came out a softer, wider streak. ACCEPT the one on the painting: at 1x it is a thin high cirrus line and gives the upper sky some movement, and a repaint over it would mean a sky-tint patch, which lesson 5 says misjudges by a value step.
- Crosses and their mounds (490-740 x 420-580): fine. Not on the list, but I looked anyway.

## Handoff, end of sitting 7 (painting at day 245; nothing new laid)
State: finished, signed, all dry. "Boot Hill, Last Light".
Reflection: my heart is happy with it. This sitting was a look-and-test sitting. The one thing that nagged me in a crop, the open grave reading a bit like a plank, got six honest scratch trials over replicas dried as long as the painting's. Each variant pointed somewhere worse: bevel, teeth, box lid, log, blade. That tells me the plain dark slit is already the least object-like way to say "hole" at this size in this idiom, and beside its heap it does say it. So I left the painting untouched, on purpose. In the gallery view the duel reads at once: the white-hot muzzle, the head shot, two dark figures against the gold afterglow, the crosses on the plain.
If ever taken further: nothing pressing. I'd leave it.
Practical lessons carried forward (hypotheses marked):
1. Light accents on dark need SET paint under them (9x). Check drying() first; 12-14 days covers round-2.x detail work.
2. blend() after a LIGHT passage on a dark figure spreads it (3x). For rim light, use one pointed round line along a scanned mask edge, with no blender. Hypothesis (1x): blending a DARK valley stroke in a ribbon about 2x its width is safe.
3. Rag lift (dip 1.0, pressure 1, refold, 3+ passes) clears a thin wet glaze but leaves an outline ghost.
4. Darkening glaze: transparent darks + medium .75-.8, hand=glaze, cov 2, fill, then blend in the same mask.
5. Hold-view matching misjudges light sky tints by about a value step. Dab trials on the spot are reliable.
6. Hypothesis: broken horizontal texture on a twilight plain reads as water.
7. No cast shadows in afterglow.
8. Flash recipe: smoke body -> set 4-9 days -> blotted white core -> tongues starting outside the core -> sparks.
9. Keep fig_all current when using clip.
10. Radiating pointed streaks read as spines or horns at splash scale (2x), but as a star at about 4u (1x).
11. A hole: its inside must be darker than the ground, and the far wall nearly as dark as the slot. Any lighter band with an edge inside a dark slot reads as a box top or bevel (3x now). A mound needs a darker base (1x).
12. Accents on a dark object in twilight should be the dark tinted toward the light, about 60/40 (4x).
13. Scratch trials: copy the painting's ground and passage at the same coordinates (a replica function with an offset) and dry them as long as on the painting. A third replica kept untouched is a useful comparator.
14. For small objects, shape carries the read more than the lights do (2x). Rounded blobs read as lumps; angular corners read as made things.
15. When reshaping a dark object over a two-part background, cover the excess with each background's own paint, split by its mask (1x).
16. NEW hypothesis (1x): a vertical light-to-dark gradient across a horizontal dark bar reads as a cylinder (a log). Tiny light tops on lip clods read as teeth.
17. NEW (1x): ground piles (flat 4, cov 3.5) over a dry dark slot cover it cleanly in one pass. Removal is a real option for a small dark shape.
18. When several variants of a repair each read worse in different ways, the original is probably the right simplification for the idiom. Accepting it is a decision, not a give-up.

The painting is still **Boot Hill, Last Light**, and I didn't add a single stroke to it this sitting. All the work happened on the scratch canvas.

A gunfighter in a long red-brown coat fires across a graveyard just after sunset. His revolver goes off in a white-hot core with orange tongues of flame. Across the leaning crosses, a hunched zombie lurches toward him on clawed hands and worn shoes, and blood sprays from the back of its skull. Behind them the blue-violet cloud runs down into a gold afterglow over the mesas, and both figures stand dark against it.

**This sitting:** I looked at the whole picture fresh and in close crops. One thing nagged me: in a crop, the open grave behind the zombie's feet looked a little like a dark plank lying on the ground. I copied that part of the painting onto the scratch canvas, dried as long as the original, and tried six fixes. Every one read as something else:
- **A lighter end wall:** looked like a bevelled edge.
- **Clods of earth at the edges:** the light tops looked like a row of teeth.
- **A lighter far-wall band:** looked like the lid of a box.
- **A warm, flash-lit end:** looked like the cut end of a board.
- **A top-to-bottom shading:** looked like a log.
- **A perspective trapezoid:** looked like a blade.

Painting the grave out entirely worked cleanly, but then the zombie would have no grave to have climbed out of. The plain dark slit beside its heap of earth is the simplest way to say "hole" at this size, so I'm keeping it as it is.

**Left as they are, on purpose:** I checked each of these again in a close crop and wrote a judgement for each in the journal. The cartoon smoke puff, the gore spray, the smooth plain, the small headstone on the horizon and a thin rippled cloud streak in the upper right all suit the picture's bold, poster-like style. A re-made cloud streak on scratch was only softer, not better. Painting a patch of sky over the real one would risk a visible ghost, because I misjudge light sky colours when mixing.

My heart is happy with it. It reads at a glance: the white-hot muzzle, the head shot, and two dark figures against the gold. The journal has an updated handoff with the practical lessons, including three new ones from this sitting:
- **Shading a dark bar:** shading it from light at the top to dark at the bottom makes it read as a log.
- **Painting out a small dark shape:** it can be painted out cleanly with the ground's own colours.
- **When every fix fails:** if each attempted fix reads worse in a different way, the original is probably already the right simplification.
